terms.grammar: ēmorior, ēmorī, ēmortuus sum, with the ablative rīsū
terms.comment: Latin dies of laughter, as English does: rīsū is the ablative of cause. Terence has the old infinitive ēmorīrī.

terms.grammar: īlia, īlium n. pl., the flanks, with dissolvō, dissolvere, dissolvī, dissolūtum
terms.comment: Not found in Lewis & Short or the loci collections in this form; Traupman is the only evidence. Lewis & Short s.v. contendō cites īlia rīsū from Ovid (A. A. 3.285), the flanks strained with laughter.

sources: Lewis & Short: ile
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 108.
